defects.summary: The depth counter does not skip characters inside JSON strings, so a brace or bracket within a string value corrupts the depth count and causes mis-extraction or failure.
defects.evidence: if t[j] == opener: depth += 1  # no check for whether j is inside a quoted string

defects.summary: Depth is tracked for only one bracket pair at a time, so a JSON object nested inside an array (or vice-versa) is truncated to the inner value instead of the outer one.
defects.evidence: for opener, closer in (("{", "}"), ("[", "]")):  # only one pair is depth-tracked per pass

defects.summary: The search always tries '{' before '[' regardless of which appears earlier in the text, so an array that precedes an object is never returned as the 'first JSON value'.
defects.evidence: for opener, closer in (("{", "}"), ("[", "]")):

defects.summary: The depth counter treats delimiter characters inside JSON string literals as structural, so a '}' or ']' within a string value causes premature termination and a failed parse of valid JSON.
defects.evidence: if t[j] == opener: depth += 1 / elif t[j] == closer: depth -= 1  — no check for whether t[j] is inside a quoted string (e.g. {"note": "}"} would extract '{"note": "}' and fail json.loads)

defects.summary: Because '{' is always tried before '[', a nested object inside a top-level array is returned instead of the enclosing array, which is the actual first (outermost) JSON value in the text.
defects.evidence: for opener, closer in (("{", "}"), ("[", "]")) — for input '[{"a":1}]' the function finds '{' at index 1, extracts '{"a":1}', and returns it, never considering the outer '[' at index 0

defects.summary: The depth counter does not skip characters inside JSON string literals, so a closing brace or bracket that appears within a string value will prematurely zero the depth and cause extraction to stop (or fail to parse) at the wrong position.
defects.evidence: if t[j] == opener: depth += 1 / elif t[j] == closer: depth -= 1  — no state tracking for being inside a "..." string or for backslash escapes

defects.summary: The loop always tries '{' before '[', so when the first JSON value is an array that contains objects (e.g. [{"a":1}]), the function extracts the inner object rather than the full array, returning the wrong 'first JSON value'.
defects.evidence: for opener, closer in (("{", "}"), ("[", "]")):  combined with i = t.find(opener) which searches from index 0 each iteration

defects.summary: Using `or` to fall back to `reasoning` will incorrectly skip a valid but falsy JSON value (e.g. `{}`, `[]`, `0`, `""`, `False`) returned by `extract_json(content)`, because Python treats those as falsy and proceeds to the second operand.
defects.evidence: obj = extract_json(content) or (extract_json(reasoning) if fin != "length" else None)

defects.summary: The summary line `-> ok/total` is indented inside the for-loop body, so it prints after every item instead of once after the loop finishes.
defects.evidence: print(f"    -> {ok}/{len(tier['items'])}")   # 8-space indent (inside loop); should be 4-space indent (after the for block, before return)

defects.summary: The docstring promises 'every distinct number' (i.e. unique values) but the code never deduplicates, so repeated values appear multiple times in the returned list.
defects.evidence: vals.append(fn(m)) / vals.append(float(m.group())) — values are appended unconditionally with no set-membership check, and the final `return vals or None` returns the raw list rather than a deduplicated collection.

defects.summary: On ZeroDivisionError (e.g. a fraction like '1/0'), the function returns None immediately, discarding all previously collected values and contradicting the docstring's stated contract that None means 'there are no numbers'.
defects.evidence: except ZeroDivisionError: return None

defects.summary: A ZeroDivisionError in any single fraction causes the entire function to return None, discarding already-collected values and contradicting the docstring's stated contract that None means 'there are no numbers'.
defects.evidence: except ZeroDivisionError: return None

defects.summary: The 'exactly one distinct number' guard is applied asymmetrically: gold uses exact set membership (len(set(gv)) != 1) while got rounds to 6 decimal places before deduplicating (len({round(v, 6) for v in av}) != 1), so two numbers in got that differ only in the 7th decimal place are treated as one, violating the invariant the docstring states.
defects.evidence: len(set(gv)) != 1   vs   len({round(v, 6) for v in av}) != 1

defects.summary: The docstring promises a "UNIT-TOLERANT" numeric compare, but the implementation uses rel_tol=1e-3 (0.1 % relative tolerance), which is far tighter than a one-unit tolerance and contradicts the stated contract.
defects.evidence: return math.isclose(av[0], gv[0], rel_tol=1e-3, abs_tol=1e-9)  vs. docstring line 'then a UNIT-TOLERANT numeric compare'

defects.summary: Using `or` treats valid falsy parsed JSON values as missing and falls back to reasoning or None.
defects.evidence: obj = extract_json(content) or (extract_json(reasoning) if fin != "length" else None)

defects.summary: The function does not deduplicate values despite docstring saying distinct.
defects.evidence: vals.append(...) calls and return vals or None

defects.summary: A zero denominator makes the whole function return None, not just skip that span or only when no numbers exist.
defects.evidence: except ZeroDivisionError: return None

defects.summary: Removing all commas can concatenate adjacent numeric tokens.
defects.evidence: t = (text or "").replace(",", "")

defects.summary: The function returns duplicate occurrences instead of the distinct numeric values promised by the docstring.
defects.evidence: vals = [] ... return vals or None
